chapter: With King Oliver in New York
title: Reading drum charts: endings and counting ahead
summary: Moore explains first and second endings, intros and the need to count bars and read ahead when playing shows.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Can you explain that first and second ending to me?

Well, the first course, you repeat the first course. You got your little dots up there, they tell you to repeat. You play the first course twice, if you want to. And you jump to the second ending, something like a modulation, something like a modulation, like, but the rhythm is still going. Then you go in, the second ending, the course, you're going into the last course. Now, you can play that second ending twice, if you want to. Or you can play it once. But the introduction is tricky. Second ending is tricky. Especially the quarter is the last course, the end of the course. That's very tricky. You got to know what you're doing. You might have two bars out. You might have three bars out. I have four. But when you, you got to count. When the drummer is supposed to be, lay out four bars, the other band is playing. But you're laying out four bars. But some of the other, the rhythm is doing something else. But you got to know when they come in, you got to be, you got to count. Otherwise, you got to count about two, three bars while you're playing ahead. You know, like you're playing here. You got to count two bars ahead. Read ahead all the time. Read ahead all the time. Two bars ahead all the time. So I like to read enough to play shows.
